occurrence.label: US munitions depletion and the multi-year replenishment cycle

title: Munitions replenishment: the three-year clock is set by rocket motors and seekers, not by the primes
thesis: Six months of the Iran war have drawn down at least four US munition families past half their pre-war inventories (about 3,000 Tomahawks with more than 1,000 expended; an estimated 2,330 Patriots with 1,060 to 1,430 expended), and the replenishment is now contracted rather than proposed: a seven-year, up-to-$35bn THAAD award to Lockheed Martin, a seven-year $22.9bn Tomahawk award to Raytheon, a $3bn Northrop framework for Patriot and THAAD components, sitting under a $70.5bn FY27 missile procurement request. The primes that receive those dollars are the most exhaustively covered names in US defence. What is not mapped is why the replenishment takes years rather than quarters: the binding constraint is upstream, at solid rocket motors, energetics and explosive fill, large forgings and castings, and specialty seekers, where the Pentagon is only now trying to widen sole-source positions from one supplier to two and where a named analyst says outright that no dollar figure overcomes the bottleneck. The chain from an appropriation to an energetics plant is the un-crowded part.
why_now: The spend crossed from request to signed contract inside three months: the THAAD seven-year undefinitized contract action for up to $35bn was awarded 2026-06-24 and the $22.9bn seven-year Tomahawk award landed 2026-08-17, raising annual Tomahawk output from 60 to more than 1,000. At the same time the physical ceiling became explicit in reporting: at the current maximum rate of 96 THAAD interceptors a year it would take 27 years to reach the quantities the Pentagon wants, amid supply chain bottlenecks for major components such as solid rocket motors. The Pentagon's own response, a $3bn framework naming Northrop Grumman as a SECOND supplier of rocket motors, is the tell: it identifies the choke point by trying to duplicate it.
retail_gap: Retail and mainstream coverage of munitions replenishment runs entirely through the prime contractors and the topline appropriation: LMT, RTX and NOC are among the most owned and most covered industrials on the NYSE, and the $70.5bn budget line is a headline number. The component layer that actually sets the delivery schedule (solid rocket motors, energetics and explosive fill, large forgings and castings, seeker optics and focal-plane assemblies) appears in defence trade press and analyst commentary, and effectively nowhere in general financial coverage. Some of that capacity is also government-owned contractor-operated, which is unreachable and must be separated out at chain time rather than assumed away.

unmappedness.rationale: The occurrence is publicly known and heavily covered: a six-month war, an inventory drawdown reported by multiple outlets, and three contract awards each announced with a press release. Selection here is not about obscurity. It is that the chain consequences are unmapped: reporting stops at which prime got which award, while the reason the replenishment takes years is one and two tiers upstream, at suppliers the coverage names only as a category. The Pentagon's own $3bn Northrop framework, whose stated purpose is to add a second rocket-motor supplier and reduce sole-sourcing from defense prime contractors, is direct evidence that the choke point is upstream of the primes and that it is currently held by very few hands. Held at 70 rather than higher because defence supply-chain constraints are a known genre of analyst commentary; what is missing is the issuer-level census, not the concept.

evidence.claim: Before the war the US had about 3,000 Tomahawk long-range missiles and likely used up more than 1,000 of them in the war on Iran; an estimated 2,330 Patriots were in stock before the war, but between 1,060 and 1,430 have been expended.
evidence.source_name: Al Jazeera, As the US restarts war on Iran, is its weapons stockpile running low?
source_excerpt: The US had about 3,000 of the long-range missiles that are fired from sea at ground targets.
It likely used up more than 1,000 in the war on Iran.
An estimated 2,330 Patriots were in stock before the war, but between 1,060 and 1,430 have been expended.

evidence.claim: At the current maximum annual rate of 96 interceptors a year it would take 27 years for defense contractors to produce THAADs to reach the quantities the Pentagon wants, amid supply chain bottlenecks for major components such as solid rocket motors, with a window of vulnerability for several years until inventories return to their previous levels.

evidence.claim: The Pentagon's FY27 request is $70.5 billion on missiles and other related line items, a 188 percent increase over what was approved for FY26, when the munitions figures for the three services combined were $24.4 billion; a named analyst expects solid rocket motors and seekers to continue to be really significant bottlenecks that no dollar figure can overcome.
evidence.source_name: Breaking Defense, The Pentagon wants a 188 percent bump for missile procurement. Can industry deliver?
source_excerpt: $70.5 billion on missiles and other related line items — $36.6 billion for the Army, $22.6 billion for Navy weapons, and $11.3 billion for the Air Force.
FY27's request is a 188 percent increase over what was approved for FY26.
the munitions figures for the three services combined were just under $20 billion in FY25 and $24.4 billion in FY26

And for munitions, I think we're going to see solid rocket motors and seekers continue to be really significant bottlenecks, and I'm not sure that there's a dollar figure that can overcome those bottlenecks.

evidence.claim: The Pentagon inked a combined $3 billion framework agreement with Northrop Grumman to boost production of critical components for Patriot and THAAD interceptors, under which Northrop will become a second supplier of rocket motors, a known bottleneck in the interceptor supply chain, with the stated aim of reducing sole-sourcing from defense prime contractors.
evidence.source_name: DefenseScoop, Pentagon inks $3B framework agreement for Patriot, THAAD components
source_excerpt: The Pentagon inked a combined $3 billion framework agreement with Northrop Grumman to boost production of critical components for Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense interceptors, government and industry officials announced Monday.
Northrop will become a second supplier of rocket motors, a known bottleneck in the interceptor supply chain.

Defense officials said the agreements are intended to boost long-term demand for interceptor component suppliers, multiply exquisite munition production and reduce sole-sourcing from defense prime contractors.
